title: They Threw Him Into a Pit… But Heaven Was Already Writing a Throne
paragraphs:
They Threw Him Into a Pit… But Heaven Was Already Writing a Throne
The Hidden Gospel in Joseph's Story That Reveals How Jesus Turns Betrayal Into Redemption—and Why Your Worst Chapter May Become God's Greatest Testimony
Some stories refuse to let go of your soul.
You don't simply read them—you somehow find yourself inside them.
Joseph's story is one of those stories.
Many remember it as the story of a dreamer who became the second most powerful man in Egypt. Others remember the colorful robe, jealous brothers, prison, or Pharaoh's palace.
But hidden beneath every chapter is something far greater.
Joseph's life is not merely a biography.
It is a prophetic shadow.
A Gospel written centuries before Bethlehem.
A portrait painted long before the Cross.
A whisper of Jesus Christ before the world ever heard His name.
Once you see it...
You can never unsee it.
Because Joseph's story is ultimately not about Joseph.
It is about the God who takes scandal and rewrites it into grace.
That has always been His specialty.
And perhaps...
He's doing the same with your life right now.

The Hebrew Scriptures introduce Joseph in Genesis 37 as יוֹסֵף (Yôsēph), meaning "May He add" or "May the LORD increase." The name comes from the Hebrew root יָסַף (yasaph), "to add" or "to increase."
Joseph's very name carries hope.
Increase after loss.
Blessing after emptiness.
Life after disappointment.
Even before his story begins, God has already hidden the message of restoration inside his name.
Joseph was deeply loved by his father Jacob.
Genesis 37:3 says,
"Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons..."
That favoritism became the seed of family scandal.
His brothers hated him.
Not because Joseph stole from them.
Not because he abused them.
Simply because he was loved.
Then came the dreams.
God gave Joseph visions of future exaltation.
Instead of celebrating God's calling, his brothers plotted murder.
Jealousy has always been dangerous.
Long before it destroys another person...
It destroys the one who carries it.
Eventually Joseph's brothers stripped him of his robe.
The beautiful garment his father had given him.
Then they threw him into an empty pit.
Genesis says there was no water.
Only darkness.
Silence.
Isolation.
A place that felt like death.
Can you imagine what Joseph must have wondered?
"God...
You gave me the dream.
So why am I in the pit?"
Have you ever asked God something similar?
"You called me.
So why did they betray me?
Why did my family reject me?
Why did everything fall apart?"
Joseph never received immediate answers.
Neither do many of us.
Because God often explains His purpose only after we've walked through it.
Joseph's brothers eventually sold him for twenty pieces of silver (Genesis 37:28).
That detail should stop us.
Joseph was betrayed for silver.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Matthew 26:15 records Judas receiving thirty pieces of silver.
Different amounts.
Same pattern.
The innocent one rejected by those closest to him.
This is not coincidence.
It is divine foreshadowing.
Joseph entered Egypt as a slave.
Jesus entered this world as a servant.
Paul writes in Philippians 2:7 that Christ "emptied Himself".
The Greek word is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from κενόω (kenoō), meaning "to empty."
The eternal King willingly took the place of a servant.
Joseph had no choice.
Jesus chose it.
That makes Christ infinitely greater.
In Potiphar's house Joseph remained faithful.
When Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce him, Joseph refused.
Genesis 39:9 records Joseph saying,
"How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"
Notice his reasoning.
He did not simply fear consequences.
He feared grieving God.
Biblical holiness is not merely avoiding punishment.
It is loving God too much to deliberately wound the relationship.
His reward for integrity?
False accusation.
Prison.
How painfully familiar.
Truth sometimes suffers before it triumphs.
Jesus also stood falsely accused.
Isaiah had already prophesied:
"He was oppressed, and He was afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth." (Isaiah 53:7)
Joseph entered prison innocent.
Jesus entered the grave innocent.
Neither circumstance changed God's plan.
If anything...
It advanced it.
One of the greatest lies suffering whispers is this:
"God has abandoned you."
Joseph's life completely disproves it.
God was with Joseph in the pit.
God was with Joseph as a slave.
God was with Joseph in prison.
God was with Joseph inside forgotten years.
Genesis repeatedly says,
"The LORD was with Joseph."
Not after the prison.
During the prison.
The Hebrew phrase is יְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף (YHWH hāyāh ʾet-Yôsēph)—"The LORD was with Joseph."
God's presence was never dependent upon Joseph's circumstances.
Neither is His presence with His children today.
Sometimes God does His deepest work where nobody applauds.
Years later Joseph stood before Pharaoh.
The prisoner became the interpreter.
The forgotten man became indispensable.
The slave became governor.
Only God writes stories like that.
But the greatest moment was still coming.
His brothers arrived.
Hungry.
Broken.
Unaware they were standing before the brother they had betrayed.
Joseph had every earthly reason to seek revenge.
Instead...
He wept.
Genesis 45 records one of the most beautiful moments in Scripture.
Joseph revealed himself.
Then he declared,
"Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life."
Notice what Joseph did not say.
He did not deny their sin.
He did not pretend evil never happened.
He simply recognized that God's sovereignty was greater than human wickedness.
Then comes Genesis 50:20.
Perhaps one of the greatest summaries of redemption in the entire Old Testament.
"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good..."
The Hebrew is astonishing.
"You meant..."
חֲשַׁבְתֶּם (ḥashavtem)
"But God meant..."
חֲשָׁבָהּ (ḥashāvāh)
The same Hebrew root חָשַׁב (ḥāshav) appears for both.
Human beings planned evil.
God planned redemption through the very same events.
Scripture does not teach that evil becomes good.
Rather, God overrules evil without becoming its author.
He remains perfectly holy while accomplishing His saving purposes through human rebellion.
That truth reaches its highest fulfillment at Calvary.
Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered up according to God's predetermined plan, yet wicked men crucified Him.
Human responsibility.
Divine sovereignty.
Both are true.
The greatest crime in history became the greatest act of redemption.
Only God could turn an execution into salvation.
Only God could transform scandal into grace.
Joseph saved people from physical famine.
Jesus saves humanity from eternal death.
Joseph provided bread.
Jesus declared,
"I am the bread of life." (John 6:35)
Joseph forgave his brothers.
Jesus prayed,
"Father, forgive them..." (Luke 23:34)
Joseph reconciled a broken family.
Jesus reconciles sinners to God.
Joseph preserved one nation.
Jesus offers salvation to every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.
The similarities are breathtaking.
Yet Joseph remains only a shadow.
Jesus is the substance.
Colossians 2:17 reminds us that the shadows point to Christ.
Every page of Scripture ultimately leads to Him.
This is why the Gospel is not an isolated message beginning in Matthew.
It is woven through Genesis.
Echoed in Exodus.
Whispered by the prophets.
Sung in the Psalms.
Declared by the apostles.
Fulfilled in Christ.
And still changing lives today.
Maybe you feel like Joseph.
Forgotten.
Misunderstood.
Discarded.
Perhaps someone lied about you.
Perhaps your own family wounded you.
Perhaps your dreams seem buried beneath years of disappointment.
Do not mistake delay for abandonment.
The pit was never Joseph's destination.
Neither was the prison.
Neither was slavery.
God was preparing a man before revealing a throne.
More importantly...
God was preparing history for Jesus Christ.
Your story may not unfold the same way Joseph's did.
Not every earthly injustice is resolved in this life.

Scripture never promises that every believer will receive Joseph's earthly promotion. Many faithful saints endured suffering without public vindication (Hebrews 11:35–40). But God does promise His presence, His sanctifying work, and the certain hope of resurrection for all who belong to Christ (Romans 8:28–39). The ultimate reward of the believer is not an earthly throne but eternal life with Jesus.
That is the deeper promise.
Not that every life will look like Joseph's.
But that every life surrendered to Christ will be held securely by the God who never wastes suffering.
The Cross proves it.
The empty tomb guarantees it.
If God can transform betrayal into salvation...
He can redeem your broken chapter too.
Not because you deserve it.
But because Jesus does what no one else can.
He rewrites everything.

If this message stirred your heart, don't let it end with you. If this exposed something hidden in your heart, comment, "Jesus, rewrite my story." If you're still trusting God through unanswered questions, comment, "I'm still waiting, but He's still faithful." Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Your support enables us to continue producing biblically faithful articles, devotionals, videos, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content that points people to Jesus Christ.

If the Lord has used this ministry to bless you, consider becoming part of this mission. Together, we can proclaim the Gospel, strengthen believers, and reach those who have yet to hear the life-changing message of Jesus.
One surrendered life can become the beginning of someone else's eternity.
